newsitem.title: USA: Former CBS executive to head Sony U.S. unit.
newsitem.headline: Former CBS executive to head Sony U.S. unit.

text.p: Howard Stringer, the former president of CBS's broadcast group and CBS News, Thursday was named president of Sony Corp. of America and will oversee a variety of operations from its retail stores to its Web site.
Stringer, who assumes his new post on May 5, succeeds Michael Schulhof, who left as president and chief executive in December 1995.

The company said Stringer is to work closely with Sony's operating companies, including Sony Electronics Inc., Sony Music Entertainment Inc. and its Sony Pictures Entertainment Hollywood studio, to coordinate group-wide efforts to expand Sony's business.

But unlike his predecessor, Stringer will not have direct oversight of those three divisions. Since Schulhof's departure, those units have been reporting directly to the top management at the parent company in Tokyo.
However, Stringer will oversee management of Sony Retail Entertainment, Sony Online Ventures and SW Networks, the company said.
Sony Retail Entertainment operates and develops theatrical exhibition sites, location-based entertainment centres and Sony retail stores.

Sony Online Ventures encompass the company's Internet site, which is used to promote its products and programmes, while SW Networks produces and distributes music and entertainment programming for radio broadcast.

A company spokeswoman said Sony was attracted to Stringer because of his extensive background in broadcasting distribution and content, as well as his recent experience with digital distribution through TELE-TV, a partnership formed by three telephone companies.
Industry observers said that background would be helpful in an era of digital technology melding with media.

"He brings a perspective of what kind of programming works for the mass market," said Gary Arlen, president of Arlen Communications, a market research outfit based in Bethesda, Md. "Sony's reach is so extensive and its brand is so strong, this becomes a critical test for Sony's ability to keep up in a business that's fragmenting."
Stringer also will become a member of the boards of directors of Sony Corp. of America, Sony Electronics, Sony Music Entertainment, and Sony Pictures Entertainment.

Most recently, Stringer was chairman and chief executive of TELE-TV, which was formed in 1994. He joined TELE-TV, which had been formed to develop home entertainment, information and interactive services, in March 1995.

Earlier this month, the partnership made up of Bell Atlantic Corp., Nynex Corp. and Pacific Telesis Group said they were scaling back TELE-TV and eliminating 100 jobs, about half of its total work force.
Stringer spent 30 years at CBS television, where he served as president of CBS Broadcast Group and president of CBS News, leaving in 1995 to join TELE-TV.

During his years at CBS, Stringer served in a variety of key editorial and management positions, including executive producer of CBS Evening News with Dan Rather. He was instrumental for luring television host and comedian David Letterman to CBS from NBC-TV.
A native of Wales who served as a sergeant in the U.S. Army during Vietnam, Stringer became a naturalised U.S. citizen in 1985.
Sony also named Ted Masaki deputy president of Sony Corp. of America. He succeeds Ted Kawai, who is returning to Japan to become senior general manager of Sony's international marketing centre.
In addition, Sony Corp. of American Executive Vice President Nick Henny will assume additional responsibilities as chief financial officer.
Masaki's appointment is effective June 1, while Henny's appointment is effective immediately.
